config.title: Build typed permissions DSL

intro.title: Build typed permissions DSL
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a typed permissions Domain-Specific Language (DSL) in TypeScript. You will create a system that defines user roles and actions, then checks if a user is allowed to perform an action based on their role. The core concept is using TypeScript's type system to enforce permissions at compile time, making your code safer and more predictable. You'll work with TypeScript interfaces, union types, and generic functions to construct this DSL. By the end, you'll have a reusable, type-safe permissions checker that can be integrated into applications.
intro.usecase: A typed permissions DSL is essential for building secure, maintainable authorization systems in enterprise applications. You'll find this pattern in admin dashboards where different user roles (admin, editor, viewer) need granular access controls to features, data, and UI components. SaaS platforms like project management tools or CRM systems use typed permissions to define who can create projects, edit customer records, or view financial reports. By implementing a type-safe DSL, developers prevent runtime authorization errors and ensure permissions logic is explicit and testable throughout the application.

objectives: Construct a type-safe permissions DSL using TypeScript interfaces
Implement permission validation functions with explicit return types
Apply union types to define hierarchical permission levels
Configure type guards to narrow permission checks at runtime
Integrate the permissions DSL into a mock authentication system
Manipulate permission sets using mapped types for role-based access
Initialize a permissions registry with compile-time type safety

steps.title: Import TypeScript type utilities
steps.instruction: Import the TypeScript type utilities 'Partial', 'Required', and 'Readonly' from 'typescript'.
steps.hint: Use a named import to bring in these three specific type utilities from the 'typescript' package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing multiple utilities
import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The code will have the necessary type utilities imported for building the permissions DSL.
successCriteria: Partial, Required, and Readonly are imported from 'typescript'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You imported some type utilities, but make sure to include all three: Partial, Required, and Readonly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. Import Partial, Required, and Readonly from 'typescript'.

steps.title: Define the Permission type
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript type alias named 'Permission' that defines a basic permission structure with 'id' (string) and 'action' (string) properties.
steps.hint: Use the 'type' keyword followed by the alias name and an object type with the required properties.
steps.seedCode:
// Import the type utilities here

// Define the Permission type here
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a Permission type that can be used as the foundation for your permissions DSL.
successCriteria: The Permission type alias is defined with 'id: string' and 'action: string' properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your Permission type includes both 'id' and 'action' properties as strings.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Permission type wasn't defined correctly. Check that you used the 'type' keyword and included both required string properties.

steps.title: Create the Resource type
steps.instruction: Define a Resource type that maps resource names to their available permissions using a TypeScript type alias.
steps.hint: Use the 'type' keyword to create a new type alias. The Resource type should be an object where keys are resource names (strings) and values are arrays of Permission.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a Resource type that can be used to represent resources and their permissions in a type-safe way.
successCriteria: A Resource type alias is defined as an object type with string keys and Permission[] values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the Resource type is an object type with string keys and arrays of Permission as values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Resource type definition is missing or incorrect. It should be a type alias that maps resource names to Permission arrays.

steps.title: Build the UserRole interface
steps.instruction: Create an interface named UserRole with a 'name' property of type string and a 'permissions' property that maps Resource to Permission[].
steps.hint: Define an interface with typed properties. The permissions property should use a Record type to map Resource keys to Permission arrays.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a UserRole interface that defines the structure for user roles with typed permissions mapping.
successCriteria: The UserRole interface is defined with name: string and permissions: Record<Resource, Permission[]> properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure both properties (name and permissions) are correctly typed according to the instruction.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface doesn't match the required structure. Check that you have both properties with the correct TypeScript types.

steps.title: Define the PermissionChecker type
steps.instruction: Define a type alias named PermissionChecker that represents a function type. This function should take a UserRole and a Resource as parameters and return a boolean indicating whether the role has permission for that resource.
steps.hint: Use the type keyword to create a type alias for a function signature. Remember to use the existing UserRole and Resource types as parameter types.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: a function type for validation
type Validator = (input: string) => boolean;
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a PermissionChecker type that can be used to type-check permission validation functions throughout your DSL.
successCriteria: A PermissionChecker type alias is defined with the correct function signature using UserRole and Resource parameters.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your function signature. Make sure PermissionChecker takes exactly two parameters: a UserRole and a Resource, and returns a boolean.
steps.feedbackWrong: The PermissionChecker type wasn't defined correctly. Remember to create a type alias for a function that accepts UserRole and Resource parameters and returns a boolean.

steps.title: Create the createPermission function
steps.instruction: Create a function named createPermission that takes a Permission object as a parameter and returns it with proper type checking.
steps.hint: Define a function that accepts a Permission parameter and returns it. Use the Permission type you defined earlier for the parameter type.
steps.expectedOutcome: A createPermission function is defined that accepts a Permission object and returns it with type safety.
successCriteria: The createPermission function is defined with a parameter typed as Permission and returns a Permission object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started creating the function, but make sure it accepts a Permission parameter and returns it with proper typing.
steps.feedbackWrong: The createPermission function is not correctly defined. It should accept a Permission parameter and return it with type checking.

steps.title: Implement the canAccess function
steps.instruction: Create a function named canAccess that takes a user, a resource, and a permission, and returns a boolean indicating if access is granted.
steps.hint: The function should use the PermissionChecker type you defined earlier to check if the user's role has the required permission for the resource.
steps.expectedOutcome: A canAccess function that returns true or false based on the user's permissions.
successCriteria: The canAccess function is defined with proper parameters and returns a boolean.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the function returns a boolean and uses the correct parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. The function should check if the user's role has the required permission for the resource.

steps.title: Define sample resources and permissions
steps.instruction: Create two sample resource objects using the Resource type: one named 'article' and another named 'dashboard'.
steps.hint: Use the Resource type you defined earlier to create objects with appropriate id, name, and owner properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: Two typed resource objects will be created to demonstrate the DSL structure.
successCriteria: Two Resource objects named 'article' and 'dashboard' are defined with appropriate properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You created at least one resource object. Make sure to create both 'article' and 'dashboard' with proper Resource type structure.
steps.feedbackWrong: No resource objects were created. Remember to use the Resource type to define 'article' and 'dashboard' objects.

steps.title: Create user role definitions
steps.instruction: Create typed user role objects using the UserRole interface. Define at least two roles (e.g., 'admin' and 'user') with their associated permissions arrays.
steps.hint: Use the UserRole interface you defined earlier. Create objects with 'name' and 'permissions' properties that match the interface structure.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have typed user role objects that can be used with your permission checking functions.
successCriteria: At least two UserRole objects are created with proper 'name' and 'permissions' properties that match the interface.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created some role objects, but make sure they match the UserRole interface structure with both 'name' and 'permissions' properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The user role definitions don't match the expected structure. Review the UserRole interface and create objects with 'name' and 'permissions' properties.

steps.title: Build the permission validation test
steps.instruction: Create a function named testPermissions that validates permissions using the DSL components you've built. The function should test different user roles against resources and log the results.
steps.hint: Define a function that uses your canAccess function with sample user roles and resources, then logs whether each permission check passes or fails.
steps.expectedOutcome: A testPermissions function is created that validates permissions using the typed DSL components.
successCriteria: The testPermissions function is defined and uses the canAccess function with sample user roles and resources.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the testPermissions function, but make sure it properly uses the canAccess function with sample data.
steps.feedbackWrong: The testPermissions function is missing or doesn't use the DSL components correctly. Try creating a function that tests permissions with your existing canAccess function.

steps.title: Add type safety with conditional types
steps.instruction: Create a conditional type named 'HasPermission' that checks if a user role has a specific permission for a given resource.
steps.hint: Use the 'extends' keyword to create a conditional type that returns a boolean based on whether the permission exists in the user's permissions array.
steps.expectedOutcome: A conditional type 'HasPermission' that enhances type safety by checking permission existence at compile time.
successCriteria: The 'HasPermission' conditional type is defined and uses the 'extends' keyword to check if a permission exists in a user role's permissions array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your conditional type uses the 'extends' keyword and returns a boolean based on whether the permission exists.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional type is missing or incorrect. Remember to use 'extends' to check if a permission exists in the user's permissions array.

steps.title: Export the DSL components
steps.instruction: Export all the types and functions you've created to make them available as a complete module. Add export statements for each type, interface, and function.
steps.hint: Use the export keyword before each type definition, interface, and function declaration to make them accessible from other files.
steps.expectedOutcome: All types, interfaces, and functions are exported, making the typed permissions DSL ready to be imported and used in other modules.
successCriteria: The Permission type, Resource type, UserRole interface, PermissionChecker type, createPermission function, canAccess function, sample resources, user roles, testPermissions function, and conditional type are all exported.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've exported some items, but not all. Make sure to export every type, interface, and function you've created in the previous steps.
steps.feedbackWrong: The exports are missing or incorrect. Review the previous steps to identify all the types and functions that need to be exported.
